title: Calibration of X-ray multimeters for half-value layer: measurement methods and uncertainty evaluation
authors: Aino Tietäväinen, Paula Toroi, Bartel Jansen, et al.
abstract: The first half-value layer (HVL), defined as the thickness of material required to reduce the x-ray beam intensity (air kerma) to 50%, is a key radiation quality specifier. Although HVL has been measured for decades using ionization chambers and aluminum filters, the detailed measurement procedures and associated uncertainties remain insufficiently established. With the growing use of x-ray multimeters (XMMs) capable of measuring HVL directly from the x-ray beam, reliable calibration and uncertainty evaluation are needed. This work presents a detailed approach for determining the first HVL and calibrating XMMs for RQR 2, RQR 5, and RQR 10 standard radiation qualities for radiography as defined in IEC 61 267. The uncertainty budget is structured into three steps: measured HVL, reference HVL, and HVL calibration coefficient, emphasizing the effects of ionization chamber energy dependence and field size. The reference HVLs for RQR 2, RQR 5, and RQR 10 were 1.417 mm Al, 2.570 mm Al, and 6.510 mm Al, respectively, with expanded uncertainties ( k = 2) of 1.0%, 1.1%, and 1.7%. The corresponding HVL calibration coefficients had uncertainties of 1.4%, 1.3%, and 1.8%.

title: Phase-resolved X-ray spectroscopy of the Vela pulsar with NICER observations
authors: E. Zubieta, F. García, S. del Palacio, et al.
abstract: PSR J0835-4510 (the Vela pulsar) is the best studied pulsar in the southern hemisphere given its high radio brightness and large glitch activity. However, its X-ray brightness is lower, making the study of its X-ray profile difficult. We aim to investigate the X-ray emission of the Vela pulsar coming from the surface of the neutron star to infer the properties of its hotspots and assess whether they share a common spectral shape. We also aim to prove whether the 2021 glitch affected the hotspots. We used an ephemeris obtained from high-cadence radio observations with the radio telescopes of the Argentine Institute of Radio Astronomy to combine all the observations of the Vela pulsar after its 2019 glitch and before its 2024 glitch. We obtained a folded pulse profile for three different energy ranges and subsequently studied their phase-resolved energy spectra. We additionally analyzed a observation to quantify the pulsar's contribution to the total soft X-ray emission detected by , which cannot spatially resolve the pulsar from the surrounding pulsar wind nebula (PWN). NICER Chandra NICER The pulsar contribution to the total observed emission represents less than 40–45% of the flux below 0.9 keV, dropping to 3–4% in the 0.9--2.0 keV range and further down to ∼2% above 2 keV, where the PWN fully dominates. We find that the X-ray folded profile of the Vela pulsar was not measurably perturbed by the 2021 glitch. We studied seven regions of the pulse profile separately. We found that all of them are well modeled by one or two blackbodies. title: Fluid Dynamic Model of Supernovae in the Time Bubble Universe Framework: Vortex Contraction, Energy Conservation, and Synchrotron Emission
authors: Mancone, Giacomo, Roberto
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: La fisica ufficiale delle supernovae (sia a collasso di nucleo che termonucleari di Tipo Ia) incontra notevoli difficoltà teoriche nel spiegare in modo unificato le asimmetrie morfologiche, i cinetismi orbitali ellittici dei frammenti e l'origine rigorosa delle emissioni di sincrotrone non termiche nei resti, dovendo spesso ricorrere a complessi modelli ausiliari di turbolenza e shock stocastico. Il presente articolo adotta come quadro assiomatico preliminare la teoria del Time Bubble Universe (TBU), assumendo la validità del modello spaziotermodinamico a bolla con flussi perimetrici. L'obiettivo di questo lavoro è duplice: (1) dimostrare che le anomalie e i problemi irrisolti della dinamica delle supernovae trovano una spiegazione semplice, geometrica e rigorosa applicando i principi fluidodinamici del TBU; (2) validare tale coerenza esplicativa come ulteriore e robusta conferma della fondatezza teorica del framework TBU stesso.

title: High-resolution 3D Inspection of Bonding Defects in HBM using Optically-coupled X-ray Computed Laminography
authors: Sung Oh Cho, Jaeyoung Im, Minjun Kim
abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence and high-performance computing has accelerated demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), in which dozens of DRAM dies are vertically stacked and interconnected through through-silicon vias (TSVs) and micro-bumps. Bonding defects such as bump voids, non-wets, and misalignment in these interconnects critically affect device yield and reliability, making nondestructive three-dimensional (3D) inspection essential. Conventional X-ray imaging systems rely on geometric magnification, which forces the use of low-power nano- or micro-focus sources and results in scan times exceeding 30 minutes per HBM module. In this work, we present an optically-coupled X-ray computed laminography (CL) system that decouples spatial resolution from the X-ray focal spot size by placing a scintillator in direct contact with the object and acquiring images through an optical magnification stage. This configuration allows the use of a high-power X-ray tube with a large focal spot without sacrificing resolution. A sub-micrometer spatial resolution was achieved using a 11-μm-thick CsI:Tl scintillator and a 10× optical lens, and 3D reconstruction of an HBM module from 1600 projections clearly resolved DRAM-to-DRAM and DRAM-to-logic micro-bumps along with bump voids. The proposed system establishes a practical route toward high-throughput, high-resolution in-line inspection of advanced 2.5D/3D semiconductor packages.

title: Ion Migration in Metal Halide X‐Ray Detectors: Mechanism, Impact, and Suppression
authors: Haoran Deng, Youkui Xu, Zhiwen Jin
abstract: ABSTRACT In recent years, metal halides (MHs) and their derivatives have emerged as promising candidates for x‐ray detection. These materials offer distinct advantages, including high x‐ray absorption efficiency, tunable bandgaps, low costs, and facile processing. While the performance of MHs‐based devices has improved rapidly, ion migration under high operating bias voltages remains a critical bottleneck. This phenomenon leads to severe degradation issues, such as elevated dark currents, electrode corrosion, baseline drift, and reduced carrier collection efficiency. Therefore, a systematic review of ion migration in MHs‐based x‐ray detectors is of crucial importance for breaking through the bottlenecks in their performance and stability, as well as advancing their practical applications. This review starts with the microscopic mechanisms of ion migration, detailing its origins, pathways, driving forces, and electrical characterization methods. Subsequently, based on energy band analysis, we elucidate the impact of ion migration on device performance. We then categorize existing suppression strategies into four main approaches: enhancing lattice interactions, minimizing migration channels, blocking transport pathways, and designing self‐powered detectors. Finally, the review discusses current challenges and outlines future development directions for stable MHs‐based x‐ray detectors.

title: X-Ray Computed Tomography and Laminography Measurements of a 3D-Stacked IC
authors: Felix Hoyean Kim, Orion Kafka, Istiaq F. Shiam, et al.
abstract: Advanced semiconductor packages manufactured using heterogeneous integration techniques challenge many conventional non-destructive testing processes. A three-dimensional (3D) structure of stacked integrated circuits (ICs), for example, complicates many existing non-destructive testing techniques. X-ray-based imaging methods, on the other hand, can fully penetrate the part and are ideal for visualizing the complex 3D heterogeneity. In this research, two related X-ray-based 3D imaging techniques, X-ray computed tomography (XCT) and X-ray computed laminography (XCL), are used to measure over-molded modules on a laminate substrate that includes stacked flip-chip Gallium Nitride on Silicon Carbide (GaN-on-SiC) dies. Differences between XCT instruments, XCT instruments versus an XCL instrument, and acquisition parameter settings on 3D reconstructions of the sample are explored. Reference measurement results are compared for image quality, acquisition time, and imaging artifacts. We discuss the current capabilities, limitations, and a potential outlook/roadmap for improving throughput for these types of instruments.

title: Analysis of Thermomechanical Fatigue Damage Progression in Short Fiber-Reinforced Composites Using X-Ray Computed Tomography
authors: Andrzej Katunin, Li-Wei Ma ., Ming Zhang, et al.
abstract: Due to the increasing applicability of short fiber-reinforced thermoplastic composites in numerous industrial applications, it is essential to develop efficient models for assessing and predicting their fatigue life for optimal design and operation of components made of these materials. Due to material heterogeneity and complex fatigue response that covers not only mechanical fatigue but also the self-heating effect, i.e. dissipative heating coupled with mechanical response, the fundamental understanding of fracture and failure mechanisms driven structural degradation of these materials is of key importance. In this study, the progression of fatigue damage under fatigue loading has been evaluated with the presence of the self-heating effect and specific fracture mechanisms have been identified using X-ray computed tomography. The character and rate of progression of fatigue damage are reported together with specific fracture mechanisms for thermomechanical fatigue loading.

title: Signatures of Lorentz violation in the bright ring for Sgr A* images from radiatively inefficient accretion flows
authors: Cuiyu Zhao, Songbai Chen, Jiliang Jing
abstract: Abstract We have investigated the effects of Lorentz violation (LV) on the bright ring in Sgr A* images illuminated by the 230 GHz thermal synchrotron emission from radiatively inefficient accretion flows around a rotating LV black hole within the low-energy Hořava gravity framework. Our results reveal that the LV parameter reduces the bright ring diameter yet increases its width, luminosity, azimuthal asymmetry and orientation angle. A higher spin parameter strengthens the LV-induced effects on the bright ring properties. Increasing disk thickness reduces the ring diameter and enhances the LV parameter’s effects on this diameter. The ring width shows no systematic dependence on the disk thickness. These quantities of the bright ring display similar trends against the black hole spin and the LV parameter for the rotating LV black hole. Using EHT observational data of Sgr A*, we find that, at fixed disk thickness, the parameter-space map illustrates that the bounded range of the LV parameter first broadens and then contracts with the growing black hole spin, and shifts toward smaller LV parameter values. In addition, the LV parameter narrows the bounded range of black hole spin: negative LV parameter values shift this range to a higher spin, while positive values shift it to a lower spin. Finally, we probe effects of the LV parameter on the peak position value and the width of the primary image and the $$n=1$$ n = 1 photon ring for the rotating LV black hole. The peak positions and their widths nearly always decrease with the LV parameter. The peak position differences for various LV parameters are more pronounced for a purely Keplerian accretion flow. In addition, the primary image and the $$n=1$$ n = 1 photon ring produced by purely radially free-falling flows are broader than their counterparts generated by purely Keplerian flows.

title:
Watching Chemistry Across Ages via Synchrotron Radiation
X-ray Microimaging Techniques
authors: Marine Cotte, Victor Gonzalez, Clément Holé, et al.
abstract: Conspectus While this special issue highlights various developments and applications of ultrafast imaging techniques, our focus here is on significantly longer time scales. Instead of examining dynamic systems at submillisecond resolutions, we explore how imaging methods can be utilized to analyze materials that are static at the time scale of data collection to trace reactions that occurred years, decades, or even centuries ago. Some ongoing reactions were quenched at the time of object creation and provide insights into the manufacturing processes used by past civilizations. Others have developed beyond the initial creation of the object, either through deliberate techniques, such as prolonged drying processes in paintings, or via incidental factors that may ultimately cause degradation. It is generally assumed that a rapid chemical reaction indicates artists’ intentions, while reactions occurring over months or years are typically viewed as alterations rather than intentional processes. Therefore, the rate of chemical reactions and their chronology is a crucial factor for scholars for distinguishing between original and nonoriginal materials. When analyzing fragments from cultural heritage objects, it is essential to assess not only the chemical nature of constituents but also their spatial distribution. This information can provide valuable insights into the physical and chemical processes involved in their formation (dissolution, diffusion, precipitation, reduction/oxidation...), as well as their potential origin. Synchrotron radiation (SR)-based micro-X-ray techniques offer both the chemical sensitivity and lateral resolution necessary for these applications. Below, we present three representative examples of study of chemical processes in heritage science. The first case demonstrates how a fragment from an artwork or a craft object can offer insights into the technical and artistic practices developed centuries ago. This is illustrated through studies that elucidate the physicochemical phenomena involved in the production of ancient ceramic glazes from various archeological contexts, such as brown glazes from Song China (10−12th-century) and luster glazes from the Abbasid Caliphate (8−13th-century). The second case examines the reactions involved in degradation phenomena, highlighting that certain heritage materials can be dynamic over periods of months or years. This example also emphasizes the importance of preparing and analyzing mock-up samples to study their evolution under natural and artificial aging conditions. This case is demonstrated with several examples of pigment degradation in paintings, with a focus on the emerald green used by James Ensor (1860–1949) and Robert Delaunay (1885–1941). Finally, the last case shows that, in some cases, attributing the origin of a chemical compound to a material intentionally used by the artist or to degradation phenomena is not straightforward. This is illustrated by the analysis of the origin of different unusual lead compounds detected in Leonardo da Vinci’s (1452−1519) and Rembrandt van Rijn’s (1606−1669) oil paintings.

title: Physics-constrained machine learning for powder x-ray diffraction
authors: Nathan J. Szymanski
abstract: Powder x-ray diffraction is the workhorse of crystalline materials characterization, yet its interpretation still relies heavily on expert judgment. Machine learning offers a route to automate this process, with progress over the past decade revealing a clear trend toward increasingly reliable models as more physical knowledge is incorporated. Early neural networks treated diffraction patterns as generic one-dimensional signals and often failed to generalize from simulated to experimental data. Performance improved as diffraction physics was incorporated first into the data and then into the models used to interpret them. In this Perspective, we trace this progression and argue that the next step is to constrain inference using computational priors. Machine-learned interatomic potentials now make it inexpensive to predict quantities such as phase stability, thermal expansion, and defect behavior, which can constrain which phases are likely to form and how their diffraction patterns evolve with changing experimental conditions. Incorporating these priors directly into the inference objective could improve the reliability of both ex situ analysis and in situ or operando measurements, and we discuss the opportunities and challenges involved.

title: Hydration-induced microstructure evolution of clay-sulfate rock characterised by X-ray computed tomography
authors: Jonas Bethge, Patrick Aimedieu, Michel Bornert, et al.
abstract: This study examines the swelling behaviour of clay-sulphate rock by observing microstructural changes using X-ray computed tomography (XRCT). Rock swelling presents a significant challenge in geotechnical projects such as tunnelling and road construction, where mineralogical changes can cause considerable structural deformation. This research investigates the microstructural evolution of clay-sulphate rock from the Belchen Tunnel (Switzerland) under different humidity and mechanical conditions. XRCT imaging reveals that water exposure leads to prominent crack formation, mainly along layer interfaces. When exposed to water vapour, gypsum crystals precipitate within cracks and on the rock surfaces, encouraging further crack growth. Conversely, complete submersion in liquid water causes anhydrite to dissolve without subsequent gypsum crystallisation. These results highlight the influence of hydric conditions on the swelling behaviour of clay-sulphate rock and offer valuable microstructural insights for assessing and managing risks in clay-sulphate-rich formations.

title: Probing synchro-curvature and pair synchrotron emission from the millisecond-pulsar population of 47 Tucanae
authors: Christo Venter, Hambeleleni Davids, A. Kopp, et al.
abstract: Globular clusters host populations of millisecond pulsars (MSPs). The collective emission from these pulsars may contribute to the observed gamma-ray spectra of the clusters. We investigate the broadband emission of 47 Tucanae using a population-scaled, phase-averaged model that combines primary synchro-curvature (SC) radiation with synchrotron radiation (SR) from secondary electron–positron pairs in pulsar magnetospheres. The calculated spectrum, scaled to an effective population of 50 MSPs, is compared with Fermi-LAT gamma-ray observations and Chandra X-ray measurements. The primary SC component produces a broad GeV maximum and a low-energy spectral tail, while magnetospheric pair SR contributes predominantly at lower photon energies. The combined spectrum approaches the observed flux levels but does not reproduce every gamma-ray data point, and the model parameters remain degenerate. The X-ray comparison provides a consistency check on the system’s energetics rather than representing a detailed model of the spatially diffuse emission.

title: Hydrogen peroxide oxidation and hydraulic conductivity evolution in fractured lignite for subsurface cultivation and gasification
authors: A.K.M. Badrul Alam, Noritaka Aramaki, Shuji Tamamura, et al.
abstract: Subsurface cultivation and gasification (SCG) seeks to enhance biogenic methane production from lignite by cultivating methanogens in situ, and its rate-limiting step is the supply of a bioavailable substrate. Hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) is injected into a fractured lignite seam to solubilize part of the coal macromolecule into dissolved organic carbon (DOC), which the methanogens then convert to methane. The same oxidation, however, also alters the lignite skeleton, so the hydraulic conductivity that governs oxidant delivery and the subsequent transport of methanogen-bearing groundwater may change during treatment; this response has not previously been resolved. A fractured lignite specimen from the Tempoku coalfield, Hokkaido, Japan, was immersed in 1 wt% H 2 O 2 solution at 22 ± 1 °C and ambient pressure for 169 days. Hydraulic conductivity, H 2 O 2 and DOC concentrations, and specimen height were measured throughout, and structural evolution was followed by sequential photography and X-ray computed tomography (CT). Hydraulic conductivity rose by 64% from its baseline value in water of 1.8 × 10 − 5 m s − 1 to a maximum of 3.0 × 10 − 5 m s − 1 on day 5; it then fell by 87% relative to that maximum to a minimum of 4.0 × 10 − 6 m s − 1 on day 89; and it recovered by 70% relative to that minimum, reaching 7.04 × 10 − 6 m s − 1 on day 169. The H 2 O 2 concentration fell from 1.0% to below 0.03%, while DOC rose to 1756 mg L − 1 , indicating extensive oxidative solubilization of lignite organics. Specimen height decreased by 41% relative to its initial value of 9.9 mm, and the fracture network evolved from dilation through closure to pore coalescence. Quantitative image analysis of the CT mid-sections showed that, between the initial state and day 169, the fracture area fraction fell by 56–60%, the fracture trace intensity by about half, and the mean aperture of the remaining fractures by 14–22%. The hydraulic response follows a chemo–mechanical sequence: oxidation → softening → swelling → compressive stress → fracture closure → partial leaching-driven recovery. A constitutive model coupling oxidation kinetics, sorption-induced swelling and fracture aperture evolution reproduces these trends. For the single specimen and site examined here, the results indicate that oxidant dosing and hydraulic cycling must be managed to sustain injectivity and microbial viability in SCG operations.

title: Gamma-Ray Modes in a Transitional Pulsar
authors: Maksat Satybaldiev, Manuel Linares
abstract: Abstract Transitional millisecond pulsars (tMSPs) exhibit a unique subluminous disk state, at the crossroads between accretion and rotation power, where they switch between two distinct X-ray modes. We present the discovery of gamma-ray modes in PSR J1023+0038, the first confirmed tMSP, from stacking Fermi-LAT data during the modes (which we identify using simultaneous X-ray observations). Surprisingly, we find that gamma rays and X-rays are anticorrelated during this mode switching: the gamma-ray flux is higher in the X-ray low mode, and vice versa. This contradicts the state-of-the-art model, which predicts bright gamma rays only in the X-ray high mode, from the interaction between the pulsar wind and surrounding disk via synchrotron and inverse Compton processes. Because the pulsar wind is likely absent in the gamma-ray high (X-ray low) mode, which is also brighter in the radio band, we suggest that jet emission may be dominant in GeV gamma rays. We also discuss an alternative interpretation where the gamma-ray high mode is powered by self-synchrotron Compton emission in the propeller state.

title: Discovery of One-Dimensional Rare-Earth Hybrid Nitrate Double Perovskites
authors: Meng-Jun Lin, Ye Xiang-rong, Lei Pan, et al.
abstract: Abstract Rare-earth hybrid nitrate double perovskites (REHNDPs) have recently emerged as an intriguing subclass of functional materials, combining structural diversity with rich intrinsic optoelectronic, magnetic, piezoelectric, and ferroelectric properties. Although notable progress has been made in three-dimensional (3D) and 2D REHNDPs, 1D counterparts have yet to be discovered. Herein, by introducing the bulky organic cation 1-adamantyltrimethylammonium (TMAA+), we report a family of 1D REHNDPs with the general formula (TMAA)2LnCs(NO3)6 (Ln = La3+, Ce3+, Pr3+, Nd3+, Sm3+, and Eu3+). Distinct from the μ2-κ3(O,O′,O″) mode characteristic of 2D and 3D REHNDPs, the bridging NO3− ligands adopt a μ2-κ3(O,O′) coordination mode in 1D counterparts. Strikingly, (TMAA)2SmCs(NO3)6 possesses a step-like high-temperature dielectric switch at 431.7 K. (TMAA)2EuCs(NO3)6 shows brilliant photoluminescence with a quantum yield of 65.46% and a lifetime of 5.21 ms. The X-ray detector based on (TMAA)2EuCs(NO3)6 demonstrates high X-ray sensitivity of 560 μC Gyair−1 cm−2 and a low detection limit of 153 nGyair s−1 under a bias of 25 V. This work bridges a critical dimensional gap and significantly expands the structural and functional portfolio of the REHNDPs.

title: Synchrotron X-ray Data of non-diseased and diabetic Human Pancreas Tissue and Islet Segmentation Model
authors: Lukas Hessel, Jonas Albers, Matthias M. Gaida, et al.
abstract: Three-dimensional virtual histology using synchrotron radiation micro-computed tomography enables non-destructive visualization of biological tissue microarchitecture with isotropic resolution. To support quantitative studies of human pancreatic morphology, we provide high-resolution 3D X-ray imaging datasets of 55 pancreatic tissue cores from 32 individuals. The collection comprises histologically non-diseased pancreatic tissue from organ donors and non-neoplastic regions of surgical resection specimens from patients with pancreatic cancer, including subgroups with insulin-dependent diabetes or following neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue cores with a diameter of 1 mm were imaged at 650 nm isotropic voxel size, yielding a mean effective spatial resolution of 1.66 µm. The cohort includes reconstructed volumes, corresponding immunohistochemistry, clinical metadata, expert-validated annotations, and dataset-specific example 2.5D U-Net models for automated segmentation of islets of Langerhans. A representative co-registered section yielded a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.81 and intersection-over-union of 0.67. This openly accessible, FAIR-compliant resource supports quantitative analysis of endocrine, exocrine, ductal, and stromal architecture and provides a reproducible reference framework for three-dimensional virtual histology of human pancreatic tissue and computational benchmarking.

title: Diverse lithologies in Bennu stones revealed using X‐ray computed tomography under pristine conditions
authors: Scott A. Eckley, Nicole G. Lunning, Evan W. O'Neal, et al.
abstract: The OSIRIS‐REx mission collected a 121.6 g regolith sample from the surface of asteroid Bennu. Preliminary examination (PE) was conducted jointly by JSC Curation and the OSIRIS‐REx Sample Analysis Team. To enable advanced, non‐destructive characterization during PE, 59 centimeter‐scale stones were individually scanned using X‐ray computed tomography (XCT) inside custom‐built containers to preserve their pristine condition. The XCT data provide three‐dimensional petrographic context that supports PE, sample processing and allocation, and subsequent scientific investigations. We analyzed 14.46% ± 0.03% (17.585 ± 0.038 g) of the total returned sample mass and document extensive lithologic diversity within the collection. The samples are divided into two primary groups, monolithic and clastic, which are further subdivided into nine lithological categories. Using XCT‐derived volumes combined with measured masses, we find that the monolithic group is denser than the clastic group, and some monolithic lithologies exhibit statistically higher average densities, likely reflecting differences in composition and/or internal structure. Shape, quantified using orthogonal caliper measurements and Sneed & Folk and Zingg classifications, does not systematically correspond to lithology. The monolithic‐dark‐veined lithology is an exception, exhibiting consistently flat, bladed shapes. Correspondence between stone morphology, defined as hummocky, angular, or mottled, and lithology varies. Using X‐ray attenuation contrast in conjunction with prior petrographic and compositional studies, we identify veins, large carbonates, candidate chondrules, coarse‐grained pyrrhotite assemblages, ~25 μm long highly‐X‐ray‐attenuating phases that possibly contain platinum group elements and surface micro‐impact craters. These results provide a three‐dimensional petrographic framework for continued characterization of the returned sample and for deciphering Bennu's origin and geological history.

title: Design, construction and application of a grating-based X-ray phase contrast imaging system under laboratory conditions
authors: Xiaojia Wei, Haowei Wang, Hongyu Zhao, et al.
journal: Journal of X-Ray Science and Technology
abstract: X-ray phase-contrast imaging enables nondestructive visualization of internal structures in weakly absorbing samples, attracting increasing interest for laboratory-based applications. However, translating this technology from synchrotron facilities to laboratory settings requires rigorous parameter optimization to overcome limited source brilliance. In this work, a practical grating-based X-ray phase-contrast imaging system was systematically designed and constructed within a standard laboratory CT chamber. Key parameters, including the grating duty cycle, phase-shift conditions, and geometric constraints, were theoretically optimized to balance fringe visibility and photon flux. The required gratings were fabricated in-house using an optimized lithography and electroplating process. Experimental results using a two-step phase-shifting method demonstrated high-quality imaging capabilities across diverse applications. Specifically, tests on cotton swabs, oxidized 904L stainless steel, and fish bones highlighted the system's versatility in biomedical research and industrial failure analysis. Quantitative analysis revealed that the system significantly enhances feature detectability, achieving a Contrast-to-Noise Ratio (CNR) of 8.5 for biological microstructures—an approximately 7-fold improvement over conventional absorption imaging (CNR 1.2). This work provides a reproducible framework and validated parameter set for implementing high-sensitivity phase-contrast imaging under accessible laboratory conditions.

title: A tri-contrast signal retrieval neural network for grating-based low-dose X-ray imaging
authors: Xu Linhai, Zhang Changsheng, Fu Jian
journal: Journal of X-Ray Science and Technology
abstract: Grating-based X-Ray imaging (GBXI) can obtain tri-contrast signals of absorption, phase, and dark-field with a laboratory X-ray source and shows a promising future in clinical applications. However, this technique needs a high radiation dose to generate high-quality contrast images. A tri-contrast signal retrieval neural network (TRNN) is presented for low-dose GBXI, consisting of contrast analysis module (CAM) and image enhancement module (IEM). The CAM combines two inception modules of different scales, allowing for more effective extraction of useful information from the phase stepping projections. The IEM is an end-to-end network structure designed to further reduce noise and improve image quality. The TRNN was evaluated using three acquisitions of one mouse obtained at different X-ray tube currents, corresponding to different dose levels. Each group adopted different X-ray tube current, representing different dose level. When the tube current was reduced by 3/4, the feature similarity index measure (FSIM) values of the absorption, phase, and dark-field contrast signals retrieved with the presented TRNN reached 0.9801, 0.9123 and 0.8898 of the standard dose group. When reduced by 7/8, the FSIM values of TRNN reached 0.9703, 0.8876 and 0.8493. By FSIM, TRNN performs best compared with the current signal retrieval techniques. This work has been helpful for the future development and applications of GBXI.

title: X-ray tomography and coordinate metrology benchmark for internal cavities in additively manufactured alloys
authors: Josselin Paccoud, Hristo Valtchanov, Eric Fournier, et al.
abstract: Abstract X-ray computed tomography (CT) is widely used for dimensional inspection of inaccessible internal geometry, but multi-modal public benchmark datasets with reference metrology remain scarce, particularly for internal cavities. This paper releases a CT--coordinate measuring machine (CMM) benchmark for wall-thickness measurements using CT surface extraction of an artefact with a complex internal cavity that is disassembled for tactile probing. Four cases span Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 625 in rough and chemically milled states. Each case includes nominal computer-aided design (CAD) geometry aligned to the CT reconstruction, CT projections, reconstructed volumes, CT surface segmentations, CMM point clouds with predefined thickness-pair vectors, and derived surface- and thickness-deviation labels. The paper defines the benchmark tasks and reporting convention and reports baseline results for reconstruction-based and CAD-informed routes. The benchmark permits validation of CT-based dimensional metrology in noisy and clean environments, including CAD-constrained surface reconstruction approaches that work entirely in projection space, such as elastic registration.

title: AI-Based Particle Size Distribution Prediction from 3D Packed-Particle Tomographic Volumes: A Comparative Study with classical Watershed Segmentation
authors: Ruhi Gupta, Mayank Goswami
abstract: Abstract Abstract Determining the Particle Size Distribution (PSD) of granular media and powder compacts is vital across condensed matter physics, geological sciences, and materials engineering. While X-ray computed tomography (µCT) captures granular microstructure non-destructively, traditional quantitative PSD estimation relies on classical morphological segmentation (binarization, distance transform, and watershed flooding), which is computationally intensive and sensitive to contact-neck ambiguities. In this work, we investigate whether a compact 3D Convolutional Neural Network (Compact3DCNN, 300,900 parameters) can predict normalized 20-bin PSD histograms directly from unsegmented 3D grayscale volumes without intermediate particle instance extraction. Using a synthetic dataset of 60 independent non-overlapping polydisperse packed-sphere volumes (483 voxels) with exact analytic PSD ground truth, we benchmark the CNN against a classical 3D Euclidean distance-transform watershed baseline on an untouched, held-out test split (N = 10, 40 train / 10 validation / 10 test). On this low-to-moderate packing regime (15%–25%), the classical watershed baseline achieved superior accuracy, attaining a mean Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) of 0.0974 ± 0.0261 voxels compared to 0.3428 ± 0.0949 voxels for the CNN (paired 95% bootstrap CI: [+0.1837, +0.3156] voxels). Measured runtime was 1.19 ± 0.27 ms per volume for the CNN on an NVIDIA RTX 3050 Laptop GPU versus 33.71 ± 7.50 ms for the watershed pipeline on an Intel CPU; however, we emphasize that this reflects disparate computing architectures rather than a controlled hardware comparison. Furthermore, comparison against an empirical training-set-mean baseline (0.6206 ± 0.2440 vx EMD on validation) confirms that the CNN learns volume-specific morphological features (0.3970 ± 0.1335 vx, a 36.0% error reduction). A controlled validation experiment evaluating direct 1D Wasserstein-1 loss training yielded substantially higher error (1.1382 ± 0.4907 vx EMD) than the primary Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence configuration, illustrating optimization challenges in cumulative L1 histogram penalties. Our findings characterize the accuracy-throughput profile in direct volumetric PSD regression and delineate key open challenges for dense granular systems.

title: Fundamental mechanisms of spatter formation during full penetration laser welding revealed by high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging
authors: Christian Diegel, Leander Schmidt, Klaus Schricker, et al.
abstract: Laser beam welding of AISI 304 stainless steel leads to spatter formation as a result of the interaction between the dynamics of keyhole, melt pool, and metal vapor. Spatter formation on the top side for partial penetration welding has already investigated in the state of the art. However, as full penetration welding is used for most industrial applications, spatter formation at the sheet bottom side is particularly critical for these applications. Spatters adhering to the inside of tubes and containers cannot be removed after the welding process and may consequently result in the rejection of the entire component. A description of the fundamental mechanisms resulting in spatter formation on the bottom side is therefore essential for developing effective strategies to reduce it. In this study, high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging is used to investigate the welding process, providing high spatial and temporal resolution of the detachment of spatters. In addition, this investigation method enables direct visualization of the keyhole, particularly fluctuations of its aperture on the bottom side. Using this method, two distinct process regimes are identified as a function of welding speed during full penetration welding with an open keyhole on the bottom side. At welding speeds below 12 m min -1 , a melt swelling forms behind the keyhole aperture on the bottom side. Spatters detach from this melt swelling and are directed opposite to the welding direction. As welding speed increases, this rear melt swelling disappears and transfers to melt accumulations on the sides of the keyhole aperture with spatter formation in lateral direction. Also, in both regimes spatters continuously detach from the keyhole front on the bottom side. Due to the keyhole aperture, the melt can only partially flow around the keyhole on the bottom side or be ejected out of the melt pool directly at the keyhole front. This promotes spatter detachment directly from the front, like the melt ejection from the front in laser remote fusion cutting. These two different process regimes appear to be primarily the result of an increase in melt flow velocity around the keyhole at the bottom as the welding speed increases. The higher melt flow velocity increases the dynamic pressure within the melt pool, forcing the melt out laterally.

title: Multidirectional x-ray phase-contrast imaging with 1D modulators
authors: Luca Brombal, Cristian David Tibambre Heredia, Ashkan Ajeer, et al.
abstract: Beam-tracking (BT) is an x-ray phase-contrast imaging technique that requires a single absorption mask, making it simpler to implement than approaches relying on two or more masks or gratings, such as edge-illumination or grating interferometry. Conventional 1D-BT, based on linear masks splitting the beam into individual beamlets, is sensitive to refraction and dark-field signals only along the direction transverse to the beamlets, while multidirectional sensitivity requires 2D masks. However, 2D masks suffer from reduced photon transmission and a quadratic increase in the number of stepping positions needed for full sample illumination, resulting in longer acquisition times. Here, we present multi1D-BT, an acquisition scheme that achieves multidirectional sensitivity in the transmission and differential phase (refraction) channels using a 1D mask, by combining two consecutive acquisitions rotated 90° with respect to each other. The method is validated on a polymethyl methacrylate test phantom and an ex vivo insect specimen, comparing multi1D-BT against 2D-BT acquisitions obtained with 2D structured modulators with (nearly) matching periods and apertures. In our experiments, multi1D-BT achieved a three times faster acquisition with similar or better image quality compared to conventional 2D-BT: the signal-to-noise ratio in the refraction signal was 35%–70% higher, and up to two times higher when compared at matched exposure time, while the contrast-to-noise ratio in the transmission signal was more than doubled. These findings indicate that multi1D-BT can provide fast, multidirectional differential phase and transmission imaging using simpler and more widely available 1D modulators, at the cost of requiring image registration between the two orthogonal acquisitions.

title: Multimodal X-ray imaging reveals hierarchical fibre mechanics
authors: Elis Newham, Alissa L. Parmenter, Jishizhan Chen, et al.
abstract: Fibrous materials, ranging from connective tissues 1–4 to engineered composites 5–8 , are vital to many biological and man-made systems, optimized to withstand complex in operando or in vivo loading. The load-bearing capacity of intervertebral discs (IVDs) of the spine depends on a hierarchical extracellular matrix, where plywood-like lamellae of collagen fibres in the annulus fibrosus contain nanometre-scale fibrils built from staggered triple-helical monomers 4,9,10 . How intact IVDs couple fibril-scale mechanics to fibre-scale organization under load remains unresolved. Here we introduce TomoSAXS, a full-field 3D small-angle X-ray scattering tomography that maps fibril-to-fibre mechanics across an intact tissue. We show that intrafibrillar molecular pre-strain (D-period stagger) is lamellar textured and tightly correlated with microscale fibre strain. Pre-strain is inversely related to fibril strain and its variability, consistent with load-sharing through molecular unwinding. Radial strain bridges and high-curvature zones at the annulus fibrosus–nucleus pulposus interfaces emerge as critical regulators of local mechanics. These findings reveal concerted fibril–fibre interactions that sustain mechanical equilibrium in the IVD, preserving elasticity and shape. More broadly, TomoSAXS establishes a platform to visualize nanoscale-to-microscale matrix mechanics across biological and synthetic fibrous materials, with applications in ageing and disease, therapeutic evaluation and the design of bio-based and bio-inspired materials.
